lesson.title: Your Own Private Slice of the Cloud
lesson.summary: A Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, is a logically isolated network carved out of a public cloud provider's shared physical infrastructure, giving you the addressing, routing, and isolation of a private network without owning any hardware.
lesson.body:
Public cloud providers run enormous data centers shared by millions of customers, all using the same physical switches, routers, and cables. A VPC is what makes that sharing feel private. When you create a VPC, the provider hands you what looks and behaves like your own network layer environment: you choose your own IP address range, you define your own subnets, you write your own routing rules, and none of your traffic is visible to, or reachable by, other customers on the same physical hardware, even though you are all plugged into the same underlying switches somewhere in a building you will never see.

The overlay network concept from earlier in the course is exactly what makes this possible. The provider's physical network, the underlay, carries packets between physical machines. On top of it, the provider encapsulates each customer's traffic inside its own packet headers as it crosses that shared underlay, tagging it so it only ever reaches that customer's own virtual machines and gets decapsulated back into the customer's original packet at the other end. It is similar to putting a package inside a labeled shipping container: the trucking network that moves the container does not need to know or care what is inside it, it just needs to read the label. Two different customers can even use the exact same private IP address range inside their own VPCs without any conflict, because the overlay keeps their traffic completely separate underneath.

A VPC has real structure you design yourself, using ideas straight out of the network layer material. You pick a CIDR block for the whole VPC, for example 10.0.0.0/16, and then divide it into smaller subnets. A common pattern is a public subnet that has a route to an internet gateway, so instances there can be reached from the internet, and one or more private subnets that do not, so databases and internal application servers stay unreachable from outside. Route tables attached to each subnet decide where traffic goes. Security groups act as a stateful firewall attached to individual instances, while network access control lists apply at the subnet boundary and do not track connection state, giving you two different layers of control over the same traffic.

Picture standing up a simple two tier web application. The public subnet holds a load balancer that accepts connections from the internet. The private subnet holds the application servers and the database, neither of which accept any inbound connection from outside the VPC at all. When those private instances need to reach the internet, for example to download a software update, a NAT gateway in the public subnet lets that outbound traffic out while still refusing any unsolicited inbound connection back in, the same asymmetry you learned about with network address translation generally.

By default, one VPC cannot talk to another, or to your on premises network, at all, which is itself a deliberate security boundary, not an oversight. When an organization does need two VPCs to communicate, or needs many VPCs to communicate with each other, they set up VPC peering or a transit gateway to explicitly bridge them. That default of isolation, and the deliberate work required to cross it, is the core security property that makes multi tenant cloud computing workable: your VPC is yours, until you choose to connect it to something else.
